listenings.text: Right, so, Mum said I have to explain the school to you before we get there, so here we go, and I am only saying it once. There are six periods in a day and there is a bell for every single one of them. Your timetable is on the app, not on paper, nobody uses paper. Recess is at eleven and it is only twenty minutes, so do not go to the canteen at recess, the line is massive. Go at lunch. Your locker is upstairs in C block and there is a trick to it, you have to lift the door while you turn the key, or it does not open. And the uniform, there is a hat rule. No hat, no play. If you forget your hat they keep you inside at lunch, they actually do it. Oh, and on Monday there is an assembly in the hall, the whole school, and it goes forever. Right. We are here. Do not look so scared.

Renato, is it? Good to meet you, mate. I am Mister Dawson, I look after Year Ten. A few things and then I will let you go. There is a timetable in this folder with your name on it, and there is a map of the school behind it. The map is not very good, but it is better than nothing. You are in ten B, so your subjects are English, maths, science, PE and geography, and there is an elective on Wednesday afternoon. Now, there are two things people always get wrong in the first week. One, there is no bell for the start of period five, so watch the clock after lunch. Two, there are no lockers on the ground floor. Yours is upstairs, in C block. And Renato, one more thing. If a teacher is talking too fast, say so. Just say, sorry, could you slow down a bit. Nobody minds. Everybody in this school has said it to somebody.

reading.rtitle: Your first week at an Australian high school
paras: An Australian school day starts at about half past eight and finishes at about three. There are six periods in a day, and there is a bell at the end of every one. Your timetable tells you which subject you have in each period and which room it is in. It is not the same every day: on Monday there are two science periods, and on Wednesday there are none. Nobody walks you to your class. The timetable is the only thing that tells you where to go.

There is a uniform, and there is no way around it: shirt, shorts or trousers, school shoes, and in summer a hat. No hat, no play, which means that without one they keep you inside at lunch. There is also a locker with your name on it, and that is where your books live. There are no desks that belong to you. You move rooms all day and you carry what you need.

There are two breaks. Recess is short, about twenty minutes in the middle of the morning, and lunch is longer. The canteen sells hot food, and there is always a line at recess, so most students bring lunch from home and buy something once or twice a week. On Monday morning, before the first period, there is an assembly: the whole school in one hall, notices, sport results and somebody at a microphone for twenty minutes.

The hardest part of the first week is not the timetable. It is the speed. Australians talk fast, they cut the ends off their words, and in a room with thirty teenagers in it nobody slows down for you. There is one sentence that fixes most of that: sorry, could you slow down a bit? It is not rude and it is not embarrassing. Almost every exchange student says it in week one, and most of them stop needing it by week four.
